name: Interview finance, set 3
description: Finance questions of the kind asked in online assessments and first rounds: loan payments, bond prices, gearing, currency forwards, option payoffs, parity, Black-Scholes delta and vega, queue priority and trading costs. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: You borrow £10,000 at 10% a year. You repay it in three equal payments, one at the end of each year.
items.question: What is each payment, in pounds to 2 decimal places?

widget.accept: £4,021.15: 10,000 times 0.1 over 1 less 1.1 to the power -3.
widget.label: Payment in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the present value of the three payments equal to the loan.

byKey.simple-interest: You added three years of simple interest, £3,000, and split £13,000 three ways. Each payment also pays down the loan, so later interest is smaller.
byKey.no-interest: You split £10,000 three ways and left out interest. Each payment must also cover a year's interest on what is still owed.

explain.text: The payment P must satisfy $P(1/1.1 + 1/1.1^2 + 1/1.1^3) = 10{,}000$. The bracket is about 2.4869, so P is about £4,021.15. After the third payment the balance is exactly zero.

items.prose: A three-year bond pays an annual coupon of 6 on a face of 100. Its yield is 4% a year, compounded annually.
items.question: What is its price per 100 of face, to 2 decimal places?

widget.accept: 105.55: the coupons and face discounted at 4%.
widget.label: Price per 100

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount each of the three cash flows at the yield and add them.

byKey.par: You priced the bond at par. It trades at par only when the coupon rate equals the yield; here the coupon is higher.
byKey.not-discounted: You added the cash flows without discounting. Divide each by 1.04 to the power of its year.

explain.text: Discount each cash flow at 4%: $6/1.04 + 6/1.04^2 + 106/1.04^3$. Those are 5.769, 5.547 and 94.234, which sum to 105.55. The price is above par because the coupon beats the yield.

items.prose: You hold £10m face value of a bond priced at 98 per 100. Its modified duration is 4.5.
items.question: About how many pounds do you lose if its yield rises by one basis point?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the market value by the duration and by one basis point.

byKey.face-not-price: You used the face value of £10m. Duration acts on the market value, which is 98% of face.
byKey.ten-basis-points: You used 0.001, a tenth of a per cent. One basis point is 0.0001.

explain.text: The bond is worth $0.98 \times 10{,}000{,}000 = 9{,}800{,}000$ pounds. One basis point moves it by $4.5 \times 0.0001$ of that value. So the loss is $9{,}800{,}000 \times 0.00045 = 4{,}410$ pounds.

items.prose: You buy an asset with £100,000 of your own money and £100,000 borrowed at 4% a year. The asset falls 10% over the year.
items.question: What is the return on your own money over the year, in per cent? Use a minus sign for a loss.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find what the asset is worth, subtract what you owe, and compare with your stake.

byKey.no-interest: You doubled the 10% fall but left out the £4,000 of interest on the loan.
byKey.no-gearing: You gave the asset's own return. Half the money was borrowed, so your stake takes the whole £20,000 fall.
byKey.sign: You gave a gain. The asset fell, so your stake lost money.

explain.text: The asset ends at $200{,}000 \times 0.9 = 180{,}000$ pounds, and you owe $100{,}000 \times 1.04 = 104{,}000$. Your stake is worth $180{,}000 - 104{,}000 = 76{,}000$ pounds. That is a return of -24% on £100,000.

items.prose: A pound costs 1.2500 dollars today. One-year simple interest rates are 5% in dollars and 3% in pounds.
items.question: What is the one-year forward price of a pound, in dollars to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow each currency at its own rate, then compare.

byKey.rates-swapped: You swapped the rates. The dollar rate goes on top, since the price is in dollars.
byKey.added-gap: You raised the price by the 2% gap in rates. The exact forward divides 1.05 by 1.03, which is a little less.

explain.text: £1 today grows to £1.03, while 1.25 dollars grow to $1.25 \times 1.05 = 1.3125$ dollars. Both must be worth the same in a year. So the forward is $1.3125/1.03 \approx 1.2743$ dollars per pound.

items.prose: You sell a put on one share, struck at 95, for £2.20. You also sell the 105 call for £1.80. At expiry the share is at 88.
items.question: What is your profit or loss in pounds? Use a minus sign for a loss.

widget.accept: -£3: £4 of premium less the £7 the put pays.
widget.label: Profit in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the premiums you took in, then subtract what each option pays its holder.

byKey.no-premium: You counted the £7 the put pays and left out the £4 of premium you received.
byKey.premium-only: You kept the premium and ignored the put. At 88 it pays its holder 95 less 88.

explain.text: You took in $2.20 + 1.80 = 4$ pounds. The put you sold pays its holder $95 - 88 = 7$ pounds, and the call expires worthless. So you lose $7 - 4 = 3$ pounds.

items.prose: On one share and one expiry, you buy one call struck at 100 for £5. You sell two calls struck at 110 for £2.50 each.
items.question: Above 110, at what share price at expiry do you break even, in pounds?

widget.accept: £120: the payoff of 10 at 110 is gone 10 pounds higher.
widget.label: Break-even in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the net cost, then follow the payoff above the upper strike.

byKey.peak: You gave the strike where the payoff peaks at £10. The position still makes money until the payoff falls back to zero.
byKey.two-for-one: You let the payoff fall by £2 for each £1 above 110. The long call still pays, so it falls only one for one.

explain.text: The premiums cancel: you pay £5 and receive $2 \times 2.50 = 5$ pounds. The payoff peaks at 10 at 110, then falls one for one as two short calls outweigh one long. It is back to zero at 120.

items.prose: At strike 100 a European call costs £7.20 and the matching put costs £5.10. The discount factor to expiry is 0.98.
items.question: What forward price does put-call parity imply, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write parity with the forward, then solve for it.

byKey.not-compounded: You added the premium gap of 2.10 as it stands. It is a value today, so divide it by 0.98 to carry it to expiry.
byKey.gave-spot: You gave the spot price, 2.10 plus 100 times 0.98. The forward is the spot grown to expiry.

explain.text: Parity says $C - P = 0.98\,(F - 100)$, and $C - P = 2.10$. So $F - 100 = 2.10/0.98 \approx 2.1429$, and F is about 102.14. The premium gap is a value today, so it is divided by the discount factor.

items.prose: You are long 50 option contracts, each on 100 shares. Each option has vega £0.12 per vol point. Implied vol rises from 18% to 21%.
items.question: What is your profit, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply vega by the vol move and by the number of options.

byKey.no-multiplier: You treated each contract as one option. Each contract is on 100 shares, so you hold 5,000 options.
byKey.one-point: You used a move of one vol point. Vol rose from 18% to 21%, which is 3 points.
byKey.one-contract: You priced one contract of 100 options. You hold 50 contracts.

explain.text: Vega gains £0.12 per option for each vol point, and vol rose 3 points. You hold $50 \times 100 = 5{,}000$ options. So the profit is $5{,}000 \times 0.12 \times 3 = 1{,}800$ pounds.

items.prose: A European call is at the money with one year to expiry. Volatility is 40% a year and the interest rate is zero.
items.question: What is its Black-Scholes delta, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $d_1$ at the money, then read the normal distribution function.

byKey.one-half: You set $d_1$ to zero. At the money with zero rate, $d_1 = \sigma\sqrt{T}/2$, which is 0.2 here.

explain.text: At the money with zero rate, $d_1 = \sigma\sqrt{T}/2$, which is $0.4/2 = 0.2$. Delta is $N(0.2) \approx 0.5793$. The vol term lifts delta above one half.

items.prose: A share at £100 will be at £130 or £80 after one period, and the interest rate is zero. An analyst is sure the chance of a rise is 60%.
items.question: What is a European put struck at £100 worth today?

options.why: You weighted the £20 payoff by the analyst's 40% chance of a fall. Prices use the risk-neutral chance, which puts 60% on the fall.
You gave each move an even chance. The risk-neutral up chance is 0.4, set by the prices 130 and 80.
You gave the payoff after a fall. Today's price weights it by the risk-neutral chance of that fall.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the up chance that makes the share's expected price 100.

explain.text: The risk-neutral up chance q solves $130q + 80(1 - q) = 100$, so $q = 0.4$. The put pays £20 only after a fall, which has risk-neutral chance 0.6. Its price is $0.6 \times 20 = 12$ pounds, whatever the analyst believes.

items.prose: A binomial tree for a share with volatility 30% a year uses monthly steps, so $\Delta t = 1/12$.
items.question: What is the up factor $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$, to 4 decimal places?

widget.accept: 1.0905: e to the power 0.3 times the root of 1/12.
widget.label: Up factor

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale the yearly vol by the root of the step length first.

byKey.no-root: You used $\sigma\Delta t = 0.025$. Vol scales with the root of time, so use $0.3\sqrt{1/12}$.
byKey.no-time-step: You used the yearly vol, $e^{0.3}$. Each step is one month, so scale the vol by the root of 1/12.

explain.text: One month is $1/12$ of a year, and $\sqrt{1/12} \approx 0.2887$. So $\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t} \approx 0.3 \times 0.2887 = 0.0866$. Then $u = e^{0.0866} \approx 1.0905$.

items.prose: Three bids rest in a book with price-time priority. A bids for 200 at £50.00 (placed 09:00) and B for 300 at £50.00 (09:01). C bids for 100 at £50.01 (09:02). A market order to sell 450 shares arrives.
items.question: How many shares does B buy?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill the best price first, then by time at each price.

byKey.time-first: You filled by time alone, A then B. Price comes first, so C's higher bid fills before both.
byKey.filled-in-full: You filled B in full. Only 150 shares are left once C and A have bought.

explain.text: Price comes first, so C's higher bid of £50.01 fills 100. At £50.00, time decides: A came first and fills 200. That leaves $450 - 100 - 200 = 150$ shares for B.

items.prose: You decide to buy 10,000 shares when the price is £25.00. You fill 6,000 at an average of £25.06, the other 4,000 never fill, and the share closes at £25.20. Commission is £30.
items.question: What is the implementation shortfall, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the decision with a paper trade of all 10,000 shares at £25.00.

byKey.filled-only: You costed the filled shares only. The 4,000 you missed rose 20p, which the paper trade would have earned.
byKey.no-commission: You left out the £30 of commission. Shortfall counts every cost of the decision.

explain.text: The filled shares cost $6{,}000 \times 0.06 = 360$ pounds more than the decision price. The missed 4,000 rose by £0.20, a lost gain of $4{,}000 \times 0.20 = 800$ pounds. Add £30 of commission for a shortfall of £1,190.

items.prose: A share is at £100, and an at-the-money call on it has three months to run. Volatility is 20% a year and the interest rate is zero.
items.question: What is the call's vega per vol point, in pounds to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Vega is the share price times the normal density at $d_1$ times the root of the time.

byKey.no-time: You left out the time factor. Multiply by the root of a quarter of a year, which is 0.5.
byKey.used-t: You multiplied by the time, 0.25. Vega grows with the root of time, 0.5.

explain.text: Vega is $S\,N'(d_1)\sqrt{T}$, and near the money $N'(d_1) \approx 0.4$. So vega is about $100 \times 0.4 \times 0.5 = 20$ pounds per unit of vol. A vol point is a hundredth of that, about £0.20, or £0.1992 exactly.
